That, for the 1948 taxation year, interest be allowed at the rate of 2 per cent per annum on overpayments of tax to the extent of $5,000 and J per cent per annum on overpayments in excess of $5,000 (no interest less than $1 to be payable); and that the rates payable on overdue taxes be increased from 4 per cent and 7 per cent to 6 per cent and 8 per cent, respectively.

The first part of this resolution has to do with the rate of interest to be allowed on over-payments, while the second part has to do with the increase in the interest rate payable to the government on overdue taxes. Until several years ago this rate was eight per cent, but it was reduced at that time; it is now proposed to eliminate that reduction and to go back to the higher rates of interest that previously prevailed.
If the overdue taxes were attributable in all cases to default on the part of the taxpayers I do not suppose any of us would waste any great amount of sympathy on the taxpayer in arrears. But the difficulty in so many of these cases is that the overdue tax is attributable directly to the fact that that taxpayer does not know that he has not paid the full tax because he has not received his assessment.

Income War Tax Act
I drew the attention of the house, in speaking to this matter on May 24, to the fact that a return brought down to the house by the Minister of National Revenue two or three months ago showed that the number of income tax returns on which assessments had not been made as of December 31, 1947, was 2,336,879, and to give the house some idea of the length of time that some of these returns had been awaiting assessment I gave this further information. For 1913 and prior years -that is to say, some of these returns have been awaiting assessment for at least four years and some of them longer-the total number awaiting assessment was in round figures 44,000. For the year 1944, the number ol returns awaiting assessment was 110,000; for 1945, 265,000 and for 1946, 1,905,000.
What happens in altogether too many of these cases is this. The taxpayer makes his return. He thinks he has made a complete return and that his tax has been paid in full. But through some departmental ruling or some difficult question of interpretation of which he was entirely innocent at the time of making his return an assessment goes out three or four years after he has made his return showing that a substantial additional tax is payable by him, and interest is imposed, not from the date of the assessment but from the date on which the tax was originally payable. If the minister would make this increased rate operative only from the date of assessment, I do not think anyone would take serious objection to it, but these heavy rates of interest are most unfair when the taxpayer has waited a long time for his return to be assessed. If we ever get to the point, as I hope we shall, where the accumulation of returns to be assessed is caught up with by those engaged in their assessment and there are no long periods of waiting, this question may not be so important; but when there is a large accumulation of returns to be assessed this is not the time to increase imposts on the tax payer by collecting additional interest charges.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend's presentation, of
course, has a superficial air of complete equity and reasonableness, but if the return has not been assessed, no interest penalty runs beyond twenty months after the date of filing the return. We have found by experience that a great many taxpayers are deliberately underpaying their tax. They compute their tax correctly but do not make full payment of the tax at the time they file their income tax return. They know they can borrow money from the government at four per cent, and
they know that, because of staff difficulties, and so forth, it may not be possible to assess their return for a year or eighteen months, and they figure it is a pretty cheap way to borrow money-at rates much less than those at which they could borrow money at any commercial bank. The interest charge of six per cent is frankly in the nature of a penalty; it is intended to induce the taxpayer to pay the full amount of his tax promptly. There may be cases, of course, in which the taxpayer honestly underestimates the amount of tax due, but after all, he has the use of the money for twenty months, so this six per cent interest charge is not too excessive a rate. A great many people cannot borrow from their own bank at much less than six per cent. I do not think there will be any serious hardship in charging six per cent for twenty months. The penalty rate only applies thirty days after the date of the mailing of the assessment. We know from experience, unfortunately, that there is a great deal of underpayment of tax presumably because it is a cheap way to borrow money from the government.
No public utility charges a rate like this.

No one has sympathy with the taxpayer who deliberately underpays his tax. I suppose it is impossible for the departmental officials to make inquiry as to the particular state of innocency of the taxpayer at the time of making his return. But surely twenty months at six per cent is too high. Will the minister, if he is going to press for this increased rate, not consider reducing the period of twenty months, which I regard as too long? If we are to accept as a government responsibility the duty of assessing all returns, I submit to the committee that twenty months is too long a period on which to charge this high rate of interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will give consideration to that. I have inquired of the chief assessor, and he tells me that the number of cases of innocent under-estimation of tax is very limited.

In the first place the budget was brought down very late in 1948. Secondly, many industrial workers have had their tax deducted from their pay envelopes. I do suggest that in view of the high cost of living, high rents and everything else, this rate is very high, and if a person has not the money to pay the penalty, a heavy debt is placed upon him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This proposed amendment relates only to the 1948 tax liability for which the individual returns will be made on April 30 of next year.
Income War Tax Act

I am inclined to question the statement that the number of persons who innocently underpay their tax is limited. From my own personal experience, every year when I prepare my form and file my income tax I find I am unable to estimate it correctly, and it is not a very complicated form. To get the thing straightened out I always have to go down to the Department of National Revenue, see one of the officials in the city in which I live, and have him check it over. In most cases I find that my figures are wrong; that I have made a wrong assessment, probably an under-assessment, although it may be an overassessment. Certainly it is not a correct assessment. Although the average Canadian does not not like to pay taxes, he does not want to get out of paying it, and he is prepared to pay it if he knows what the correct amount is. When he files his return he can make out a cheque and pay the tax. It is not right that he should have to wait sometimes four years, as has been pointed out here. As of December 31, 1947, some 2,336,000 people had not been assessed. The explanation of the minister is not good enough, and I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) that the resolution be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after: "no interest less than SI to be payable." That would leave the interest rates as they were.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand my hon. friend's amendment. He is suggesting that we allow the provision to remain in the Income War Tax Act under which anyone who chooses to do so may not pay his tax, and thus permit people to borrow money from the government at four per cent per annum until such time as the income tax department are able to assess his return. That is the effect of the amendment. I am leaving aside the question whether the amendment is in order or not. I will discuss that in a minute.
The effect of the amendment is this. What the hon. member is saying is that anybody in this country can file his income tax return, pay five per cent of the tax and pay only four per cent interest on that return until the assessors are able to reach it. I do not think that is in the public interest. I do not think a four per cent rate on unpaid taxes is sufficient. Perhaps the six per cent rate is somewhat higher than the commercial rate, but I do not think it is an excessive rate. I think it is a rate which should be put in the act in order to constitute a real deterrent to the sort of thing that is mentioned. It is perfectly true, as my hon. friend has said, that it is difficult for people accurately to estimate the tax, particularly if they have a complicated type

of income, including a lot of dividends and income from other sources, and so on. I readily concede that it is difficult, particularly as applied to types of income where one is allowed to take certain deductions for depletion and so forth. But the information I get from departmental officials is that the amount of under-estimating is far greater than can be accounted for by innocent under-estimating. The cases of genuine under-estimating are of relatively small amounts, and the amount of interest which is involved is not a significant factor. By this amendment we are trying to get at the taxpayer who deliberately refrains from paying the full amount of the tax which he knows is due, realizing-
Perhaps he cannot pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whether he can pay or not-realizing that it will be physically impossible for the income tax department to catch up to him for a year or eighteen months. That is the sort of practice that I do not think should be encouraged, and that is why we are putting the six per cent rate in here instead of four per cent.

Should the minister not provide for the case that he has referred to? I agree that a person who has intentionally withheld amounts from the department might be treated as a person who is attempting to escape his duty; but the minister has not told us what proportion of the taxpayers fall into this group. What I am saying is that the law, as it now stands, permits any income taxpayer in this country legally to get an unsecured loan from the government at the rate of four per cent a year. I say that is not proper; it is not in the interests of the taxpayers who pay their taxes promptly. I say that it should not be open to any taxpayer who wishes to do so, because he has not the money on hand at the moment, or because he wants to buy a new motorcar, to file his return showing he has a tax liability of $2,000, $3,000 or $4,000, send in $1,000 on account and say: "Well, they will not be able to assess my return for a year or a couple of years, and in the meantime it will cost me only four per cent interest." Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is not treated as a criminal; moreover, he is left with the use of his money.

Yes, at four per cent. Is it not possible, without going into a great deal of additional expense or vastly increasing the personnel of the departmeitt which has to do the collecting of the income tax, to send out a notice advising the individual that he has paid less than he owes and putting him on investigation? Then he can go, if he must, to an accountant. He has some means of protecting himself against the penalty imposed upon him without his being aware of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend's suggestion is not a bad one, but one must assess the return before one knows there is an underpayment. The gravest abuse is not on the part of those who substantially underestimate the amount of tax but on the part of those who underpay the amount of the tax they estimate when they send in a return. They send in a return showing that they owe x dollars, and they pay only ten per cent, and they say: "I will wait for a while, and when I am assessed I will pay it". In the meantime it costs only four per cent interest, and that, I have suggested to the committee, holds out too great an inducement to take advantage of an easy form of borrowing at a rate of interest which compares favourably with highly secured loans in any commercial institution. That is why the rate should be six per cent. There is no question of anyone being a crook or doing anj'thing that is improper. That is what the law sa,ys they have to pay, and delay in assessment is provided against. Everyone knows that with 2,000,000 taxpayers, and with the difficulties under which the staff has to work, it is not possible to assess returns within less than six months, and in some cases considerably longer, depending upon the complexity of the return. Actually, I am told, they are on the average only about two years behind. In the case of small income-tax payers, where for the most part salaries and wages are involved, notices of assessment are out within three, four, five or six months, and that is being gradually cut down as increased staff is taken on in the Department of National Revenue. The situation is, that because of the

physical limitations involved in the assessment of returns, it is not possible to assess them all within a month or two after they are filed. There is a limitation of twenty months in respect of liability for interest. If the department cannot assess the return within twenty months, interest stops then, so that the maximum penalty is six per cent for a period of twenty months on the underpayment of taxes, when the return has not been assessed. If hon. members will think it over they will, I believe, come to the conclusion that the penalty is not an unreasonable one to put upon the underpayment of taxes.

This change in the Income Tax Act arises, I believe, from the lack of consideration, on the part of the government, of the human factors that should be kept in mind. People today are caught between rising prices and heavy taxes. In my opinion they are greatly overtaxed, especially in the income tax field. We know that the machinery for the collection of taxes is not as efficient as it might be, and this change which the government has proposed is merely a whip to make people pay. I suggest that the committee should vote for the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. John-Albert.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

May I deal briefly with 'the small taxpayer. Today he is paid through his weekly envelope or monthly salary and deductions are made at the source; in fact, ninety-five per cent of his tax is collected in that way. There is really no opportunity for him to have large means at his disposal. On the other hand, the businessman receives a form and he is asked to estimate from the previous year his income for the current year. speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I should like to say a word in reference to that matter. It is the object of the department to have the business in such a position that the returns of one year will be assessed before the returns of the next year come in. For the year 1946 there were
3,566,000	returns. That is a great deal of business. That constituted 600,000 more returns than for the year 1945. The reason for that was that the men in the defence forces had returned to Canada. During the time they were overseas they were not taxable. They had returned and had gone into business or into some type of money-earning occupation, as a result of which they had become taxable. In addition to that, this large number of returns indicates a high level of earnings by the people of this country. Over 600,000 more returns were received in the year 1946 than in the year 1945. For the year 1947, returns for which were made at the end of May, there are many hundreds of thousands more than the 3,566,000 for 1946. I think it is fair to estimate that for the year 1947 there will be at least 3,800,000 returns, or somewhere between that and 4,000,000.
When the hon. gentleman says a great number of returns for years back-as much as four years-have not been assessed, he is not speaking according to the facts. If the percentage is taken, it is exceedingly low. There are reasons for that. All during the war years the staff of the taxation division was greatly undermanned. Business came along and took from us our trained assessors, auditors and chartered accountants. Why was that? Because of the level of the salaries, for the most part, that were being paid to those who were in the salaried positions in the taxation division. That has been changed. We have a great many more assessors. We have added to our personnel something over 2,400 people throughout the country, so that we are now getting to the stage where we believe that, within one to two years from now, we shall have the assessments made on a current year basis. At that time there may be a change made, so that if the assessment is not made in a period less than twenty months, the interest rate will not apply. At the present time we are approximately twenty months to two years behind in some cases, but that condition will be improved as time goes on.

It was interesting to hear the senior member for Halifax speak from the point of view of the businessman, of whose situation he has intimate knowledge. He was probably accurate in what he said with regard to the purely business basis of this tax. But I do not think he showed any great accuracy or
knowledge of the situation as it affects those others for whom we have been speaking. I refer to the small taxpayer, and particularly to the farmer, who does not make his return on a quarterly basis-
I dealt with the small taxpayer.

-and who has no knowledge of interest or why he should be charged interest when the error was made in good faith, and particularly when the time lag is not his fault. That is our main objection to this particular piece of legislation. One must appreciate what the minister is trying to do with regard to those who deliberately underpay their own assessments. But I do not think any legislation is good which, because of a certain situation of which a few people are taking advantage, hurts everybody simply so that those few people will no longer be able to take advantage of it. The suggestion we have been making is that the particular offenders should be dealt with, instead of the whole mass of honest taxpayers being penalized, as large numbers of them will be penalized under this legislation.
I wish to refer to a case as an illustration of what happens. A certain taxpayer, a farmer, in 1943 asked to be permitted to go on a different basis. He had been on a cash basis and wanted to go on an inventory basis. He received permission, furnished information back to 1936 and established his inventory as of that date. A few months ago he received a final assessment showing that he had some $1,100 additional taxes to pay because of the additional income which that change in the method of assessment involved, from 1936, and requiring him to pay an interest penalty on the unpaid taxes of $500, or nearly half of the tax arrears. I believe that particular case is to be adjusted, but I refer to it as an example of what happens when assessments are late and when the government insists on charging interest on taxes which are in arrears for no other reason than that the assessment has been delayed.
The amendment which we moved has been ruled out of order, but I think we shall have another one which would take care of the situation. I ask the minister again to consider whether it would not be advisable, rather than to pass this new resolution in its present form, to provide that the interest penalties shall apply only to those who underpay their own assessments. That is the group to which he referred and on which he based his argument. That is the group which is obviously, shall we say, taking advantage of what he says has been a low interest charge by the government in the

past. But certainly some taxpayers have been charged interest when the twenty months' period has been exceeded and when the delay has not been their fault. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not a question of penalizing honest taxpayers, as I have tried to explain. This is a complex subject, and it covers all taxpayers. One of the ways in which substantial advantage can be taken of a low interest rate was touched on by the senior hon. member for Halifax. In the case of businessmen, they have to estimate their tax for the coming year. They estimate it on the basis of last year's tax. They are entitled to do that. Then they pay one instalment. Then, for one reason or other they do not pay the second instalment or the third. They know pretty well the chances are that, while last year was not such a good year, this year will be pretty good. There are many ways in which that can be done, and it is not illegal, but it enables a man to use money in his business which properly belongs to the government.
The cases of small taxpayers, about which so much has been made here, where they under-estimated the tax, honestly and otherwise, are usually pretty small. They might run to S25 or $50. The interest on that, even if it were $100, is only S6 for the first twelve months. And somebody can calculate rapidly what it would be for the next eight months.
All that is being suggested in the proposed amendment is that the present rate of four per cent, which I consider is too small or too low to accomplish the purpose for which it is placed there, should be placed at six per cent.
The hon. member for Eglinton suggested that consideration might be given to reducing this period of twenty months to a somewhat lower figure. My colleague the Minister of National Revenue has already touched upon that. Perhaps, if additional staff were obtained in the department and greater headway made, that period might be reduced in another year. But I say, as I said before, I think this is a section which it is in the public interest to have, and it will not cause hardship to anyone who pays his honest bills. Incidentally, this applies only to the 1948 tax period, returns for which will be filed next year.
How long has the twenty-month period been in existence?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Two or three years. I cannot remember offhand, but I am told it is up to and including 1945.

In support of the second part of this resolution which deals with an increased rate of interest on overdue taxes and provides an increased penalty, the minister has told us that the purpose of the resolution is to prevent under-payment where payment is due. He mentioned a class of persons who, he says, when April 30 comes around, decide to spend their money to buy automobiles or for some reason other than paying their taxes. He says these people do not pay the full amount of their tax when they file their returns. There may be some people like that, but there is another class of people, the people who from year to year endeavour as best they can to rake up the money with which to pay their taxes when
Income War Tax Act

they become due. However, a man may meet with a misfortune. For example, his child or his wife may go insane. He may not live in the central part of Canada where he can get the best of medical treatment, and therefore he must bring his wife or child to Montreal or Toronto or some other place where specialists are available. He may have to go to much more expense than he can really afford. It seems to me that his first duty is to his family and not to the government. He must spend the money upon those in whom he is interested in order that they may have the necessary treatment. Then a man may have his property destroyed or meet with some other misfortune.
These people do not fail to pay because they do not want to pay; they do not pay because they need the money foT some other purposes. It seems to me that they are entitled to consideration. This may be a minor class, the same as those who want to buy an automobile.
As the minister knows, these returns are usually changed in some particular from year to year. It is difficult to make out a return correctly, but the average man attempts to do it. He computes what he owes and then he pays it. That is really a difficult task for the ordinary citizen. Then, after some considerable period of time he is informed that he has not paid sufficient taxes and this excessive rate of interest is imposed. These people should be protected and, in order to protect them, I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops:
That the resolution be amended by adding to clause 2 the following words:
"That the said rates shall become payable only from and after the date notice of assessment has been sent to the taxpayer by registered mail."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Obviously I must take the same legal objection to this amendment as I did to the other. The effect of the amendment would be that any obligation of a taxpayer for payment of taxes to the crown would bear no interest until such time as the notice of assessment was mailed to the taxpayer. I think it will be recognized that it would be physically impossible for any income tax department to get notices of assessment out to the great majority of taxpayers within less than two or three months, even at the best. In the interim the taxpayer would have the free use of money owed to the government for that period, whatever it might be. I think this amendment is, beyond question, one that affects the balance of ways and means and is therefore out of order.

While the government is responsible for ways and means, the house has

the fullest freedom to criticize it, and that freedom can be exercised by way of a motion to reduce the amount of taxation. Earlier this afternoon Your Honour read the first part of citation 497, to be found on page 182 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, but I should like to read the second part of that citation, which is as follows:
But the house enjoys complete freedom to make every representation possible to the government with regard to the manner in which the ministers discharge this responsibility. This duty the members may perform by moving amendments to reduce the taxes proposed by the administration.
Although this actually does not reduce the tax, it reduces a proposed increase in penalty, and I submit that it falls within the same paragraph.

I should like to read
citation 511 of Beauchesne, second edition, which is as follows:
Each resolution can only be dealt with by being agreed to, reduced, negatived, superseded, or, by leave, withdrawn . . .

speechtext:

further and read citation 500. Before we get through, we shall have read the whole book. Citation 500 reads:
Though it is the function of the committee of ways and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes, example of the repeal of taxation effected in this committee are to be found upon the journals. have been successful in business in this dominion. They are just as much entitled to consideration as the little man.

speechtext: May I just reply to the hon. member by wishing him today a happy birthday.

But about the
results from the book. I would ask the minister this question. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The rate used to be eight per cent instead of the six per cent we are now proposing. Following discussions which took place in the house, it was decided two or three years ago that eight per cent was excessive and we lowered the rate to four per cent. The indications are that the lowering of that rate has resulted in a greater deferment of payment of tax than existed before. It is, of course, hard to pin that down. The arrears may be due to the fact that there are more taxpayers and more taxes due. Nevertheless, there is a greater amount of taxes not paid on the due date, and my advisers believe that the four per cent rate may have had something to do with that, because it was easy to borrow the tax money until the assessment could be made and notice of the assessment sent out. I dare say that all of us at some time or another have got a little bit behind in our taxes. I know that on occa-

sions I have had to go to the bank and borrow money to make my tax payment. That is the only answer I can give to my hon. friend. This was not aimed at any particular group. Obviously the salaried man or wage earner, as the senior member for Halifax has pointed out, has not much chance to get behind in his payments because they are deducted at the source. The man who does have the opportunity is the professional man, the lawyer, the doctor, the businessman, the corporation and so on. I think it is fair to say that experience has shown that the low rate of four per cent has, to some extent, encouraged the deferment of payment of taxes which are due.

I am not going to take up any time, but I believe that the Minister of National Revenue is today engaged in a definite campaign to secure payment on a widespread scale from farmers throughout the country. The campaign in the western provinces has been very direct. Numbers of individuals working for the department are going from farm to farm, and going back over the records of farmers for a period of several years. As a matter of fact, I think this additional penalty will in the main fall on farmers who, over the years, may not have been paying taxes 'because they did not have the returns that made possible the payment of taxes. First, they are allowed a write off on off-property expenses for exploration purposes, which under ordinary circumstances, under ordinary rules, would be capital expenditures. In toto.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I suppose the minister would say it is only with respect to drilling for natural gas, oil and minerals that this deduction could apply. speechtext: I do not know that I can give my hon. friend an answer at once. I agree with what has been said by the minister in connection with resolution
3.	I believe he has accomplished many things by placing this provision in the act, and making it applicable to gas and oil wells. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The matter was discussed at some length. The hon. member for Regina City pointed out that the drilling of wells for water in certain sections of Canada, particularly his own section, involved a very considerable capital expenditure, because they have to go down to great depths.
Hon. members in the committee will realize that this question of capital expenditures in connection with the drilling of wells for water, or other things, is a broad one. I have taken careful note of the representations made. Perhaps I should say to the committee that

Income War Tax Act
it involves an important principle, namely the distinction between capital expenditures and expenditures for revenue. Obviously these expenditures made for deep-test oil wells are capital expenditures, and they are so recognized in this legislation. This special tax concession, or whatever one cares to call it, is a special type of legislation to encourage this particular type of search for petroleum. I have serious doubts as to whether one can employ that general principle in connection with capital expenditures in drilling for water or other things. The matter has been brought to my attention, however, and I shall consider it.
You cannot get milk without water.

I was going to say something about water. Can the minister say whether a well bored on a farm, from which a man gets water, can be depreciated. I have an idea that it can be, but I am not sure. I believe it is two or three per cent a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know what the rate would be; but a capital expenditure of that kind, creating a capital asset, could of course, be depreciated in accordance with the appropriate rules for that type of asset.
I think it is provided at five per cent.

There is just this further point in connection with the matter. I have upstairs a letter from a man who complains that he spent about $1,200 in drilling a well for water, and that he failed to get water. He had to go ahead and drill another one. He was not complaining about the second well from which he got the water, but he did complain bitterly when he was not allowed anything in respect of income tax in connection with the dry well. He was of the opinion that the expense he had in drilling that dry hole should have been considered for income tax purposes, and that he should either be able to depreciate it over a period of years, or be allowed it as a straight expense. Could the minister give us any information or tell us what might be done in those circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot do that offhand. I could not give a definite answer. This question, of course, as to what

is a capital expenditure, and what proportion of it can be charged to current income, is one of the most difficult and complex parts of any income tax law. In the revision of the old act and the preparation of the new this one thing has perhaps given us more difficulty than almost any other. I certainly would not want to hazard any offhand opinion here in committee as to what rule should be followed.
Speaking generally, the rule is that a man has a right to depreciate capital assets over the earning life of the capital asset. Depreciation is allowed at varying rates on varying types of asset. Whether a dry water-hole could be written off in the same way as off-property exploration for oil I would not undertake to answer offhand.

If you get water you can depreciate on the basis of the tubing you put in and so forth. I think that is the basis upon which it is worked. You can write off a certain amount of depreciation, but apparently you cannot charge a hole that is dry as an expense for income tax purposes. It is just a dead loss, and this does not seem fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may be. I do not know offhand just on what basis one could justify a deduction from income tax, which means a deduction from federal revenues, for an unproductive capital expenditure. If you accepted that principle I think you would have to expand it to a much wider field than the drilling of wells where you do not find water. The general principle on which depreciation is allowed is that you depreciate on the cost of a productive asset. The theory is that you take something which is a wasting asset, and you are entitled to get your capital back and not pay a tax on income for something that is not income. In a good many cases people, make capital expenditures which are unproductive; risk capital is ventured in things which do not produce results. The fellow who risks it has to take his loss.
Drilling a well on a farm does not come under that.

Let me tell the minister a thing or two. He said that he would not like to give an answer offhand, but it should not be necessary to give an answer offhand. For at least three years the united farmers of Canada and the Alberta farmers' union have

Income War Tax Act
been submitting briefs along this line. They should have given the minister and his predecessor and the departmental officials an opportunity to discuss this matter among themselves and to have a reply ready.
I leave that for the moment. The minister has said that venture capital put into the digging of a well that turns out to be unproductive is a difficult thing to allow for purposes of taxation. Granted that it is, but by this resolution we are giving exactly that privilege in connection with exploration for oil. If you strike, oil you usually strike something that is productive for a long while. That oil will be used to operate cars and machinery and do many other things. That may be used to operate cars and machinery and do many other things. That may be much more spectacular than the pail of water which goes into a cow or a horse, but we must not forget that if you strike all the oil in the world and do not have enough water your oil will not do you much good.
You have to have beef to move around in your trucks that are being operated by your gasoline. You have to have many other things to be used in a similar way. When a man puts capital into digging a well and gets a dry hole it is a serious matter. Anyone who knows anything about farming knows how difficult it is to haul water in a tank for long distances. It is an expensive and arduous farming operation, one that must be carried on in both winter and summer.
We need stock in this country. The farmers can only do what the oil people do, survey their land and get an expert with a willow or some other fellow to try to find water the best way he can. Even with all the advice or experts they can get, they sometimes do not get any water after drilling many hundreds of feet. It cost a lot of money to do that. If there is no water it means that they have either to return to the old method of tanking or else to try again. Eventually it may mean the difference between a prosperous farm, one that is just barely getting by, or one that is actually going in the hole.
If the minister is not prepared to give an answer tonight I suggest that he give serious study to the submissions made last year, the year before and, I think, the year before that
by the farm organizations and to the representations made here tonight.

I should like to say a brief word about this. First, there is probably nothing that is more important to Canada, today than the development of a real oil field. We have indications of an oil field in Alberta that may possibly become a major-field. This is the first time in- our history that such a statement can be made. The oil is apparently a heavy type crude, which would seem to indicate a large reservoir of oil. Great possibilities open up for that part of Canada, and when I say that I ask the committee to think of the effect on the whole of Canada. If we can develop a major oil field a great part of our dollar difficulties as well as those facing our whole economy can be solved, because we shall be able to produce the essential fuel to drive the machinery of this country and to utilize the petroleum industry in a way we have never been able to do before.
I am entirely in favour of this resolution.
I should have liked to have it made a permanent part of our tax law. We have the indication, and it is certainly the hope that a major field at Leduc will be developed. As yet we cannot say that is the case, but it is encouraging. The development of a major oil field takes usually a matter of years, not just one or two. That is so, despite the surprising successes recently in Texas and in California in previous years. The development of an oil field represents hundreds of millions of dollars of venture capital. I say that advisedly, because that is what it has cost to develop major oil fields throughout the world.
I want to suggest to the minister and to the committee that those who, in the years to come, will make available the venture capital which we hope and pray will develop an oil field, should be given encouragement that, if they lose, they will at least be able to get back their venture capital if they are successful elsewhere. I think that is all anyone who risks capital can ask. If he loses he loses, but if he loses in one place and hits oil in another he should be able to recoup for his dry wells through the wells which are producers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am glad that my hon. friend has brought up that point. The main purpose of this resolution is to make statutory the provision in the Income War Tax Act with respect to the deduction of travelling and other expenses from salaries and wages received by railway employees. The general rule of the Income War Tax Act for years has been that salaries and wages as such are net income, but an exception has existed to that rule since away back in the early 1920's with regard to certain railway employees who were paid on a mileage basis.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Or on an hourly basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. By a ruling, that was extended last year to other groups of railway employees doing similar work such as parlour-car conductors, pullman attendants and so on. It seemed equitable to extend the provision to those who are engaged in the transportation industry. Those who were engaged in that industry, railway conductors and drivers of buses, for example, have to leave their home at a given day and go, let us say, from Montreal to Toronto and stay there overnight. They have to pay for their board and lodging overnight, and come back to their homes the next day. The same thing applies to pullman conductors and parlour-car conductors. I suppose the same thing applies to men operating busea
Does it include truck drivers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, transport drivers. The effect of the proposed amendment is to give statutory recognition to what has been recognized in the last year or so by an administrative ruling of the Department of National Revenue. It is being restricted, as I say, to people who are engaged in that type of activity. It is being done, because it has been
recognized in the case of these workers over a great many years that this is a proper type of allowance. In a good many other cases it can be charged as an expense, or it will be paid for by the employer and charged as an expense by him. In certain other cases it is included in the wage scale, but in the case of railway workers that wage scale or salary scale has become pretty well fixed by tradition, and does not include any provision for board and lodging expenses of this kind. That is the purpose of this proposed amendment. I cannot recall whether my hon. friend had any other question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Before the minister leaves the point of railway workers, will he answer one or two more points for clarification? He spoke of the line that was drawn until perhaps a year and a half ago between railroad train conductors on the one hand and sleeping-car conductors on the other. I take it that it is now quite clear and statutory that sleeping-car conductors get the same benefit as train conductors. There was one other group that was always a problem, namely the sleeping-car porter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are included. The proposed legislation which will be based on this resolution covers workers engaged in that industry. It will cover such people as porters, sleeping-car conductors, travelling telegraphers who have to be sent away overnight for purposes of relief and so on. It covers those engaged in this particular field because of two things: first, because of the nature of their work, and, second1, because of the particular wage structure in that occupation.
The second point which the hon. member for Eglinton referred to had to do with the question of commissions. This will allow a deduction from gross commissions of expenses incurred in earning those commissions, if the nature of the commission earner's salary is such as to require him to pay his own expenses and perform his duties away from his employer's place of business. In that case expenses may be deducted from the commissions or other fees. It seemed reasonable that that should be done. It could not be deducted:, of course, from salary; it could only be deducted from the portion of his remuneration which was based on commissions.

Why do you put this in statutory form?
Income War Tax Act

I am glad that the minister is taking the action proposed with reference to pullman conductors and others. I wonder if he will just clarify one point. He has indicated that the administrative ruling which was made about a year ago is to be given statutory effect by the resolution. I should like to be sure that there will not be any conditions introduced in the statute that would narrow the effect of the administrative ruling, because that was a good and sound ruling. In looking at the equities of the situation, I think it was fair. I may say I had some occasion to go into it, because I was acting for a number of these pullman conductors. I want to be sure that there will not be any condition attached by the statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend that it is fair. There will not be any conditions in the statute. I think that, under the law as it stands, there was no statutory justification for the ruling which was given. I question whether the law as it stands justifies that deduction. As I have said, this proposed amendment is to give statutory recognition to a practice which has prevailed for twenty-five years in connection with the running trades which are paid on a mileage or hourly basis. It will be extended to others who perform similar services but who are paid on a somewhat different basis. It will cover trainmen, engineers, parlour-car conductors, parlour-car porters, and others of that kind, who, in the performance of their duties, are required to be away from home overnight, but it will not apply-it never did apply-to train crew on yard engines, for instance, who are operating switching engines in the yards.
I may say I discussed this matter at some length with the representatives of the railway brotherhoods, and they assured me that, in the case of yard enginemen, yard trainmen, yard foremen and so on, they were not entitled to claim deductions of this kind, and were not claiming them. It is for those whose duties require them to be away overnight in the performance of those duties. They can claim their actual expenses for board and lodging.
The doubt expressed by the minister as to the-
Who is doing the talking, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Eglinton has another question.

A doubt has been expressed by the minister with respect to the legality of the ruling. I take it that it will not be intended on this statute coming into effect to upset the ruling which was applied in earlier years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no, of course not.

I want to ask the minister two questions. The questions have to do with two different parts of this resolution, and I shall ask them one at a time, if I may. The minister said that all the running trades on the railroads, also bus drivers and truck drivers who are required to be away from home are included.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they are engaged by a transport company.
Yes, of course. That would apply also to air transport crews?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Does it apply to water transport crews, crews on canal boats or lake seamen, or even seamen on the salt water?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. This applies to what I might describe generally as the overnight type of employee, the man who is not away for extended periods of time. The others should be taken care of now either by the employer or by the wage scale. But there are a great many transport workers, railway employees, bus drivers, truck drivers, aeroplane pilots and so on, who have a home at a given place where they spend most of their time, but their duties are such as to require them necessarily to be away overnight at the end of their run, and they have to make an expenditure for board and lodging which, if they could go home at night, they would not have to make. For instance, it does not apply to deep-water seamen who may be away for four or five months at a time, or, to a lesser degree, to those who operate on the lakes.

I thank the minister for that answer. The resolution goes on to say:
. . . and where a taxpayer is employed to sell property or negotiate contracts . . .
It almost looks as if it refers to one who is engaged in the sale of real estate. I notice

Income War Tax Act
that it does not say goods or merchandise. I wondered why it was worded in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told by my legal advisers that property is all-inclusive there, and as a lawyer I would agree with that. It includes property movable and immovable. It is intended to describe in the resolution the sale of tangible assets; and negotiation of contracts refers to such things as arranging the sale of an insurance policy, and that sort of thing. The essence of it is that if a man is engaged on a commission basis and receives his remuneration in the form of a commission he may deduct from those gross commissions the expenses he is put to in earning them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have one other question with respect to the other part of this resolution. The hon. member for Eglinton just asked the minister whether his doubt about the legality of the administrative order would have any continuing effect. Perhaps I should ask my question of the Minister of National Revenue. Has that administrative order been carried out in the last year and a half or the two years that it has been in effect in all parts of Canada? The reason I ask that is that one has sleeping-car conductors and sleeping-car porters speaking to him about these matters on the train. Although the men in the west learned of the provision and were able to take advantage of it, I have learned that sleeping-car conductors and porters on the trains in the east, in the city of Montreal, for example, were not allowed that deduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I find that hard to understand, because the railway brotherhoods, after the ruling was made either last year or the year before, sent out a circular. I have a copy of it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: So have I.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That circular went to all their employees, and I believe my colleague will confirm me when I say that the income tax inspectors have recognized that ruling since that time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There is no doubt but it was supposed to apply to 1947.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it applies only to 1947.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the commercial traveller is exclusively on a commission basis he gets his expenses anyway, and has always got them. He is entitled to deduct his expenses. In the case of the ordinary commercial traveller who is an employee, it frequently happens that the employer pays his expenses. He goes away on a trip and keeps track of his expenses and turns them in to his employer, and when he returns, those expenses are paid. They are an expense of the employer, and not income of the employee. This relates to the independent operator, the fellow who is not engaged as an employee by anybody but operates pretty much as an independent agent on a commission basis. He is entitled, and quite properly so, to deduct his expenses. The ordinary commercial traveller who works for X company is entitled to turn in his expense account to his employer, who pays the account, and that is not part of his taxable income.

I do not suppose the minister wants this to apply to members of the House of Commons. They are in the running trade, however, because the member is required to be "absent from his home," especially those from the maritime provinces, for long periods. The language of this resolution refers to the man whose duties "require him to be absent from his home regularly, in which case expenses for board and lodging may be deducted". I wish to warn the minister that he may be involved in a legal contest in the supreme court, and therefore I should not like to see him pass this legislation too hastily.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We members of parliament are engaged in all kinds of running.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Many people run but do not get here.

5.	That the 15 per cent income tax on nonresident persons be extended to apply to patronage dividends paid on or after May 19, 1948.

Approximately how many people will be affected by this provision, and what is the estimated amount of revenue involved?
Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot say; but I should think it would be small, because most members of co-operatives are residents of Canada, and consequently the patronage dividends they receive would be income in Canada. It was felt, however, that there might well be members of co-operatives who would be in receipt of patronage dividends while living outside Canada, and since patronage dividends are income in the hands of residents of Canada, it seemed appropriate that nonresidents who receive them should pay the regular non-resident tax, which is at present fifteen per cent on income received from Canada. I have no information as to what the amount would be. I should think, from general knowledge, it would be pretty small. It appeared to be the logical move. Since recipients of patronage dividends in Canada include such dividends in their income for tax purposes, it seemed only proper that nonresident recipients of similar dividends should pay the regular non-resident tax, which is fifteen per cent. The recipient can take credit for it in his income tax return in the country in which he resides.

I thank the minister for the statement he has made, but I am curious to know what brought this matter to the attention of his advisers. What caused them to deem it necessary to bring this in? Surely there must have been some reason that prompted the minister's advisers to suggest it.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have inquired about it, and I do not know that there was any special reason that brought it to the attention of my tax advisers. But, as members of the committee know, these tax questions are under constant consideration, particularly by officers of the finance department, whose special job it is to be considering representations with respect to tax matters, and legislation in connection therewith. It was suggested to me that it was appropriate that this type of income should be subject to the nonresident tax, patronage dividends being subject to taxation. This is a comparatively new departure. It is only in the last two or three years that we have had this provision in the act. That is the only explanation I can offer. We have always taxed dividends going abroad, and the purpose of this is simply to make sure that the technical provisions of

the act shall cover patronage dividends as well as dividends paid by ordinary stock companies.

Once again I thank the minister, but I may say to him that I would feel much happier if he could assure me that the action taken a year or so ago in taxing patronage dividends was not simply the thin edge of the wedge. Can he assure me that there will not be a gradual extension of this line of taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no. It was not the thin edge of the wedge. I do not think there has been any serious suggestion that patronage dividends should not be considered as income. Those of us who are interested in the cooperative movement have recognized that patronage dividends received by the owners of a co-operative are income and subject to taxation. That has not been questioned. There has been serious difference of opinion as to whether some other things should be subject to taxation, but there has been no question that patronage dividends are properly income and, as such, taxable in the hands of the people who receive them. All we propose is that the non-resident who receives dividends of this kind should pay the same non-resident rate of taxation that any other non-resident pays in respect of income received from Canada. That is all the amendment does.
I have no desire to protect the non-resident, but I was interested to know what brought this on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is nothing else behind it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before we come to the detailed consideration of these resolutions, there is a brief statement that I should like to make on one aspect of them. When I introduced the resolution at the time of my budget address I announced that it was proposed to suspend temporarily the British preferential duties on cotton and rayon piece goods in order to enable Canadian consumers to obtain larger quantities of these essential materials at reasonable prices. As I stated then, we have received assurances from the United Kingdom that the reduction in landed prices made possible by any removal of duties would be passed on to Canadian buyers and that the United Kingdom government would take all possible steps to see that the target which has been set for shipment to Canada of 80,000,000 yards of cotton piece goods in 1948 will be met.
I explained also that, in acordance with our commitments in the Geneva trade agreement, under which preferential margins may not be widened, the proposal to suspend the British preferential rates on cotton and rayon piece goods includes a reduction in the mostfavoured-nation rates on these items by the same amount until July 1, 1949. However, in the case of scheduled countries imports are limited by quota under the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act.
It is expected that the proposed temporary suspension of duties will have a generally beneficial effect in helping to make available larger quantities of important supplies needed by our consumers. It is proposed that the suspension should remain in effect until July 1, 1949, when the whole matter could be reviewed in the light of the results achieved.
It has been thought desirable, however, that there should be some provision whereby this matter may be reviewed from time to time before that date. In the light of the widespread dislocations which exist in international trade and the many uncertainties which prevail, particularly with regard to the effects of the consequent reduction in the most-favourednation rates made necessary by the Geneva agreement, it is felt that the governor in council should have the authority to withdraw the suspension in part or in whole if, by any chance, the assurances given are not lived up to, or if it is found that the reduced duties are in fact operating in a manner detrimental to Canada. As far as we can see now, we do not expect that any difficulties will arise which would make it advisable to use this authority, but I think hon. members will agree that it is prudent to make provision for unforeseen developments in the unsettled circumstances of

today. For that reason I would ask my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, to move an appropriate amendment to the resolutions which I tabled on the night of the budget
address.

I take it that the temporary suspension in no way affects Canada's status or Canada's right to maintain the status quo ante. By suspending these duties Canada is not yielding up her right to reimpose them, by reason of this temporary action?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. That is quite correct. In fact, as a result of the amendment which I will ask my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, to move, we shall not ask that the statutory rates as contained in the tariff be changed. The Geneva rates are in effect, as hon. members of the committee know, by order in council. They have been given provisional effect and they will remain in effect for the time being until the house decides whether or not the Geneva agreements will be approved. But there will be no change in the customs tariff so far as the rates in schedule A are concerned. The effect of the proposal which I am making is that the duties on cotton and rayon goods be suspended until July 1, 1949. Since, under the Geneva agreements, we are bound not to widen the preferences which exist in favour of the United Kingdom, this means that the same treatment must be extended to the most-favoured-nation countries, which include, as hon. members of the committee know, France, Belgium and most of the western European countries.
The only significant proposal that I am making in the proposed amendment is that, in view of the unsettled conditions and the possibility that assurances which we have received would not be lived up to-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: From whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-and the fact that we have to extend these tariff suspensions beyond the United Kingdom to these other countries, the government should reserve the right, in the event of some unforeseen development occurring, to cancel this suspension. I do not anticipate for a moment that this will be necessary, but it seems only prudent to reserve the power if some unforeseen development should occur which would be detrimental to the interest of Canada, and that we should have the right to do that. Hon, members will recall that these duties were suspended during the war by the War Exchange Conservation Act of 1940. In effect we shall be continuing the same practice here; it is a

Customs Tariff
suspension, not a removal. I did not suggest in my budget address that this should be a permanent thing, because we must see what we do about the Geneva treaties. What I have proposed-and, of course, what I am still proposing-is that these duties should be suspended for a little more than a year from now. But when we are committed under the Geneva agreements, which have been given provisional application, to extend that treatment to a great many other countries as well, it seems to me that it is prudent to reserve some discretion empowering the governor in council to suspend the suspension, if I may put it in that way, with respect to some or all of these tariff items, should unforeseen circumstances arise.

I should like to ask two questions. The first is this. If our markets were flooded from some source of supply which is not on our horizon now, or if serious unemployment should result, a remedy would be at hand?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A remedy would be available. Frankly, I do not anticipate any such contingency, because the situation with respect to textiles, as most hon. members know, is that in most lines they are in exceedingly short supply. There is nothing in the information I have 'been able to get-from any of my expert advisers on this matter to indicate that any such condition as my hon. friend suggests would arise. But the world is in an unsettled state; this special suspension is being extended to a great many countries besides the United Kingdom; and I think it is the part of wisdom to retain this power. I should say, as I have said already, that I do not contemplate that there will be any necessity to exercise it; I can see nothing on the horizon which would make it likely that we should. But I think it is the part of wisdom to do that.

The second question I wish to ask is this. Is the power to terminate the law by order in council to 'be incorporated in the act, or is it to be dependent on the continuation of controls and the general law under which they are perpetuated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It will be incorporated
temporarily in the act. The amendment, which I will ask my colleague to move, restricts the suspension of duties, as I indicated in my budget speech, to July 1, 1949, and provides that the governor in council be empowered at any time to withdraw in whole or in part the suspension in duty provided for; I am quoting from the proposed amendment, in paragraphs (a) and (b). That is the safeguarding clause to which I am referring. It will be incorporated in the customs tariff.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister made a fairly plausible argument for the proposed amendment, particularly when he used such words as "prudent"; but I confess that with me it is only plausible. Frankly I do not like it. The minister said a moment ago that there was some similarity between what he is asking for now and what happened during the war. There is a similarity, 'but it is in reverse. During the war the government, by virtue of the wide powers it had under the War Measures Act, took off certain duties. The minister is now asking for peacetime, order in council power to put on certain duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are seeking the power to suspend them, with the right to reimpose them at any time at the discretion of the governor in council.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am tiying to get away from the use of double negatives and talk in terms of what actually happens. I do not think it is completely comparable. Also, I do not like the continued extension of the delegation of authority to the government in this way. It seems to me that we are getting to the place where we make laws in this parliament, but we make only the laws that the government brings in, and then we put loopholes in them to give the government a chance to change those laws in between sessions. I did not expect this legislation to come up, so that I have not case histories in front of me. But most hon. members 'know we have had a great deal of manipulation of tariff policies in this country by both parties that have been in power down during the years. I can think of many an editorial which the Winnipeg Free Press has run on this subject, and in which it has pointed out that, whereas parliament has passed certain tariff rates, by administrative methods the effective rates have been changed.
We have, in addition to that way of changing the will of parliament, another way, namely this, the provision that by order in council this tariff which is now being removed for a period of thirteen or fourteen months can be-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Suspended.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, suspended, but so far as the effect during the fourteen months is concerned; it is off, just off. Just ask the
Customs Tariff

hon. member for Beauce, and he will tell you it is off. I am glad to see the hon. member for Winnipeg South in his seat, because I am sure that as a Liberal he will welcome this removal of tariffs on certain British goods, if only for a period of fourteen months. And I do not think he will feel very happy about the government now taking by order in council, for reasons which may seem good to them, the power to put those tariffs back on before that time is up. I shall not take further time to argue the matter now, but it does seem to me to be a little extreme and a little strange to have still another move like this from a Liberal government.
If the Liberals believe in freer trade policies and start to move in that direction, then why back up? Why leave the back door and several windows open as a means of getting out? I would much rather that parliament would endorse the proposal the government made that these duties be off from now until July 1, 1949, and that we make it definite for that period of time, with only the one over-riding exception that always holds, namely, that parliament could change it. The house will be meeting in the meantime, possibly this fall. At any rate the government can call parliament together at any time, and I feel that the supremacy of parliament in the matter should be maintained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I say one word in reply to the hon. member. I wish to point out, as I did in my budget speech, that the purpose of this suspension of duties is to assure a supply in Canada which is needed, at a reasonable price. Before agreeing to recommend it to parliament, I received assurances from the board of trade of Great Britain that they thought they could assure us that advantage would not be taken of the reduction in duties by British manufacturers, and added on to the price. I have no doubt, of course, that those assurances will be lived up to. Nevertheless the action was taken with the assurance that certain things would be done.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is also good Liberalism.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is understood that the Canadian consumer would get the benefit, and that we would get the supply.
There are other countries which benefit from this suspension, but from whom it was not possible to get similar assurances. I think it is only reasonably prudent to retain the power to remove this concession if it does not produce the results which we expect and believe it will produce. That is the reason for this suggested amendment. I do not think it will be necessary to do this.

I should like to make
it quite clear that the questions which I put to the minister, and which he has been good enough to answer, are not to be interpreted as indicating in any way any change in my unalterable opposition to government by order in council. I say the tariff should not be subject to alteration by order in council. I merely wish to make my position clear in the matter, even though I have asked the minister for some explanation concerning the amendment which he is about to introduce.

speechtext:
Does the resolution
carry ?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I understand you have not yet put the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I move the amendment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The only part that implements the suggestion just made by the minister with respect to giving power to the governor in council is paragraph (c)?

speechtext: That is right.
