speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I think there are some others who wish to speak about this. Are there any copies available?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not too complicated. If the hon. member will turn to page 4094 of Hansard for May 18, he will find that subsection 3 contains the resolution which is now amended. It is really not so complicated. The substantial effect of the amendment is, as I have indicated, that the duties on the tariff items enumerated in the resolution with respect to rayons and cotton goods, are suspended until July 1, 1949. There is a provision that the governor in council may be empowered to withdraw in whole or in part the suspensions of duty for which provision is made in the resolution. I can assure my hon. friend that is all the amendment accomplishes. The resolution is long, with an enumeration of tariff items, and a technical description of the things covered. That is all there is to it.
I have explained to the committee the reasons why I am suggesting that this amendment be put forward.
The minister is recommending definitely that the tariff be removed up to July 1, 1949?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
The governor in council, then, has no authority to make any changes in that schedule?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
Until July 1, 1949?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but it may remove this suspension-and I should like, if possible, to get away from the double negative. If unforeseen conditions arise such as I have indicated, the governor in council may withdraw this special privilege which is extended to a very considerable number of countries if, to put it bluntly, they do not live up to what we fully expect they will honour and live up to.
You may by order in council put an end to the law?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The normal tariff would then come into effect again.
In other words, if the amendment carries and if the governor in council so desires, next week or next month it may change the whole thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It can; it would revert to the regular tariff.
Next week or next month?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
I do not like that. Surely this House of Commons can see at least a year ahead. This house will again be in session-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is better than some of the rest of us, then.

It will be in session in 1949. The policy being pursued now is a Liberal policy. In other words, you are living up to the Atlantic charter, and the provision in it for free access to raw materials of the world-some of the beautiful slogans on which we fought the war.
Surely we are in a position in the House of Commons to say we are going to legislate that far ahead with respect to a restricted number of items as between ourselves and the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But I have a sort of constitutional objection to removing the tariff on an item and then allowing the fellow in the other country just to take that into his price. That is one of the main reasons why we should reserve this right. If other countries do not fulfil the assurance they have given us, then we would have the right to withdraw the special concession we have extended ito them. That is all this is.

I still cannot see that. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, it is a continuation of government by order in council. Parliament should be supreme in matters of this kind, and I do noit think the matter is serious enough, as far as the schedule under discussion is concerned. As far as I am concerned, as a member of this house I do not intend to delegate in peacetime the authority of the House of Commons to someone behind the scenes. I am going to be quite frank and say that when the minister and his advisers drafted this budget I believe they received some fairly decent Liberal advice, but I am afraid-I hope this is not true-that considerable pressure has been exerted upon the minister to leave in this escape clause. I think the amendment is
Customs Tariff

actually an escape clause designed to protect manufacturers of this country who are afraid-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has not been any pressure at all.

-that they may not be in a position to compete with those who believe in free enterprise and unrestricted trade and competition and all the other things that are supposed to enter into our economy. I consider this matter serious enough for this House of Commons to refuse the amendment. I have confidence enough in the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce and their advisers to think they will be able to do business with the countries affected by this tariff change without delegating any authority to anyone outside the House of Commons to change the law tomorrow if he so desires.
I am prepared to have it run until the House of Commons meets again, say in June, 1949. If in the interim there is any difficulty I do not think it would be so serious as to affect the country to an extent where we should be prepared to abrogate the rights of the House of Commons. There is a principle at stake. That principle is the right of this house to retain in peacetime the power to pass Jaws and have them remain effective until such time as the house may convene again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is nothing new about this, since the same sort of thing exists all through the tariff schedule. I am not an expert on tariffs, but I have before me tariff item 62, which reads:
Rice, uncleaned, unhulled or paddy . . . The governor in council, when satisfied that Australia can supply Canadian requirements, may, by order in council, direct that there be substituted for tariff item 62 in schedule A of the customs tariff, and the enumeration of goods and the rates of duties of customs set opposite the said item in schedule A the following . . .
As I say, this is not a new departure,. As I have said before, I think, under existing circumstances, this is a wise provision to insert.
Let us try it for a year and discuss it the next time we meet.

I feel that the legislation as it appears before the amendment is ill-advised, because of the effect it may have upon employment in those centres where large numbers are engaged in the textile industry. Much as I regret it, I feel that this house is constantly belittling itself when, without any reason at all, it yields up to the governor in council its hard-won supremacy in matters of legislation.
Just a few days ago we saw fifty pages torn from the merchant shipping act, when many articles having to do with the life, safety and

well-being of crews and people on ships as well as the ships themselves could be suspended by order in council. This was done to enable a servant of a department to determine that something like an emergency existed and then suspend the law.
We are a highly industrialized country, dependent to a greater extent upon foreign markets than practically any other country. We must sell at home and abroad, or we cannot continue to exist. We have increased our capital equipment and our industrial plant, We must find markets, and the best market is always the home market.
Is where you find it.

I am not going to debate that point with the hon. gentleman, because I think he will admit that the best market is the home market. If this legislation is denying occupation to our own people, then it is short-sighted. If we are to introduce into our fiscal and trade policy the same uncertainty that exists in other realms of public affairs; if we are to create in that realm the chaos which exists elsewhere I fear that we are in for a sad and sorry time.
We should know for at least one year what our tariff legislation is to be. I submit that, surrounded as the minister is with competent officers and men of some experience, he should be able to see at least twelve months ahead or until the house meets again. Laws which are vital to our economic existence and to our trading position should have some stability and not be altered until reasons are given in open debate.
We are spending time in committees devising ways for the introduction of democratic government as it obtains here. Yet we have become disrespectful of the very elements of democratic government; we delegate to some gentleman in the Department of Finance the power and the right to determine for you, for me and for the people whom we represent what shall be the fiscal policy of this country. I believe that is wrong and we shall rue the day we have openly and without necessity accepted that principle.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The case has been stated so excellently by the hon. member for Stan-stead that little more needs to be said. But I feel that we should register, in the best way we can, a protest against this request of the minister for this power by order in council. A moment ago the minister cited an example from the tariff schedule he has before him. Even though I was not able to follow it as closely as I might have, I understood that it did prescribe certain conditions under which the governor in council would have the author-

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
ity to make a change. That is not the case in connection with the amendment now before the committee. I have now been able to get a copy of it, and I find that clause (c) of the proposed amendment moved by the Minister of National Revenue reads as follows:
(c) The governor in council be empowered at any time to withdraw in whole or in part suspensions in duty provided for in paragraphs ta) and (b).
I submit, along the lines already argued so well by the hon. member for Stanstead and others who have taken part, that this parliament should not give that power to the government at this time. I therefore move, seconded by my colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the following sub-amendment:
That clause (c) of the proposed amendment be deleted.
In other words, I do not try to disturb any other of the changes made by the amendment or in the schedule attached thereto which the minister has proposed. I only ask that this special order in council power be not granted by the house to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am very glad my hon. friend has moved that sub-amendment, because I want to make it perfectly clear that the amendment is not one on which the government lays any particular stress, and I give it to the committee for what it is worth. I think it is in the interests of this country that the government should retain this discretionary power under these exceptional circumstances; but let me say this, that if the committee feels that we should give this unrestricted suspension of duties until July 1. 1949. I am not going to stand up strongly in opposition. I give it as my considered opinion, after having given the matter a good deal of consideration, that it is the part of prudence to retain that discretionary power, but I am going to lay the responsibility for voting for or against it squarely on the members of the house. I personally shall vote against my hon. friend's amendment, but if the committee sees fit to adopt it, that is all right with me.

The situation is this. The minister, in introducing this change, is not sure how it will work out. and he wants the power given to him to change it at a moment's notice if it works out badly. That is an instance of the risks which this government is willing to run with the economy of the country. Here we have a tariff change introduced by the government, and now they ask power by the amendment to undo the tariff change at a moment's notice if it should turn out that it works against the interests of Canada. If they have not examined the whole situation so care-
Customs Tariff
fully that they can say to us that this tariff change is bound to work in the best interests of Canada, the tariff change should not have been introduced and should not have the support of the house. It convinces me of something I have suspected for some time, that this whole change is ill-conceived and not designed to work in the best interests of Canada's economy. I think we should oppose the change and the amendment, and I propose to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is all right with me. As I explained this proposal, it is for the purpose of endeavouring to ensure a supply of cotton and rayon textiles to Canadian consumers at reasonable prices, and we had the assurance from the main source of supply that advantage would not be taken of this tariff concession to boost prices. I have no doubt that this assurance will be carried out. But on second thought I consider it wise to have a safeguard in case the assurance could not be carried out, or in case concessions given to other countries did not work out. But if the committee feels that this concession should be continued until July 1, 1949. without any such safeguard, that is all right with me. It is no government issue so far as I am concerned.

I support the minister's attitude in this matter. We are living in a world of bewildering complexity; no one can foresee what the situation will be one month ahead. Surely members of the house realize that. I find myself at a loss to understand the attitude taken by the two speakers of the C.C.F. and of the Progressive Conservative party. So far as leaving power in the hands of the minister is concerned, we have to leave power in the hands of ministers in regard to every aspect of our government, and we can hold them responsible if they misuse that power. Consequently I am going to vote against the sub-amendment of the C.C.F. I think it is just plain foolishness.
There is one more aspect. We are dabbling around with a whole lot of experiments in nondiscrimination and a whole lot of other things involved in the Geneva trade treaties. No one has seen those treaties in operation. How can we foretell how they will work out? Certainly it is the part of merest prudence to give the minister power to do whatever seems fit to him under the circumstances.

I should like to make one or two observations, following what the hon. member for Stanstead had to say. His anxiety and that of a good many members of this house is to get parliament back as
Customs Tariff

quickly as possible into the position where parliament is supreme. I think we are all agreed on that. During the last four or five years of necessity we had to have many things done by order in council and we had to depend on the ministers' deputies for their advice in matters of great concern. I should like to make this observation now', that we have been very fortunate in the calibre of the men who have served the different departments of government, and particularly the Department of Finance and especially those charged with this work. I pay tribute to these men. Most of them are still advising the ministers.
What bothers me now is the statement made a couple of moments ago by the minister, who said he "thought" this was necessary. I wrote the word down. If he thinks it is necessary because he has been advised by a capable civil servant who knows all the ramifications of each individual item and knows what is for the general advantage of Canada, why not have the intestinal fortitude to stick to it? We have had a welter of orders in council under the War Measures Act and the transitional powers act; and if, after all that, it is necessary to give the minister this power I think the committee ought to be broad-minded enough to grant him that power until such time as the economy not only of Canada but of the whole universe irons itself out.
My private enterprise friend the hon. member for Cape Breton South rose in his place and, with his tongue in his cheek, championed the cause of free enterprise. I say to him that when he was talking a moment ago he probably had in his mind the same idea that is in the minds of all the rest of us, and that is, in the final analysis, are we to be able to keep the employees of the textile organizations working steadily right through the piece, not only till July 1, 1949, but from there on? In common with him there are not only hon. members anxious about that, but the personnel behind the Minister of Finance, whether they say so or not, when they deal with these items are thinking of its effect on the employment of men and women in industry. They do not say so, and we do not say so often enough, but they are thinking, will it make more employment, will it make more production for Canada or will it not? From that angle they very often give their judgment.
I would suggest to the minister that when they are thinking about how they are to frame orders in council or frame advice to the minister, one of the first things in the back of their minds-at least I hope it is one of the first things in the back of their minds-is, will it give more employment, or will it maintain
fMr. Harris (Danforth).]
the present employment level in Canada? That is what they think about, or at any rate that is what they ought to think about. I charge them now with that responsibility. I am hoping, when we consider this, that we can perhaps see the end of the rainbow where parliament will again be supreme. It is almost there now. We will help you, Mr. Chairman, to put it through. But in these troubled world affairs which we are now trying to unscramble, let us be a little bit patient. Ninety per cent of the unscrambling of orders in council has been completed. We are now at the tail end of it. I ask the minister to accept some of the advice of those who served us so well during wartime. Accept their advice here and there, and depend upon them. I am of the opinion, sir, that if we do that we shall come out on the right side of the ledger.
In closing, I would say this to the minister, if I can get him away from his other conversation, from the Hollywood sort of atmosphere that envelops him now and again, to the realities of his responsibility as Minister of Finance. When his advisers advise him on such and so I remind him that he is one of the senior ministers of the crown in Canada. Mr. Chairman, I was addressing myself particularly to the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry; I was interrupted.

I know he hears, whether he listens or not. When he acts, he acts because his responsible advisers have recommended action. His responsibility to parliament is not only to think but to act and to stick to that, so that Canada itself will say: Well, we have a strong government which means what it says.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have that.

speechtext: Does resolution 3 as amended carry?

There are some questions I wish to ask with regard to the resolutions as a whole. In the first place these resolutions purport to contain the exact text of the amendments that are proposed to be introduced into the customs tariff. I have been in the house for only four sessions, but this is the first time I have seen resolutions purporting rto give the exact text of the proposed legislation. Before we proceed with the resolution, I would ask the minister to give assurance that if the committee does approve the resolution there will be no suggestion, when we come to the bill containing legislation in exactly the same form, that we do not enjoy the usual freedom in connection with the review of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will gladly give that assurance. Although I have been in the house for eight years, in that period there have not been any extensive changes in the customs tariff, and I have not had a great deal of experience myself with tariff matters. There will be a schedule to the bill amending the customs tariff, which will have to be considered in the committee item by item. I give my hon. friend the assurance that there will be full opportunity on the bill, if it is deemed necessary to do so, to discuss the matter item by item. The general principle, as I indicated in my budget address, of the changes here is, with the exception of the textile items where the tariff is suspended, to make certain downward revisions, chiefly in connection with matters of a technical nature, productive goods and the like. I outlined in general terms in my budget speech the nature of the tariff changes. By reason of the amendment which has just been passed, there will not be incorporated into the customs tariff schedules the Geneva rates with respect to any of the items. These will be dealt with in due course when the agreements, which are now before the committee or before the house itself, are approved.

One other point. It has to do with the proposed sections dealing with the power to suspend the dumping duties. I refer to the proposed repeal of section 6 and the substitution of a new section. We have had some discussion tonight about the powers proposed to be given to the government under legislation of this kind. I think the committee ought to realize, in passing the resolution, that it proposes to give the
minister the power to suspend certain duties of a special dumping nature. The committee ought also to be aware that the classes of goods with respect to which this power is to be conferred on the minister are not defined in the section. The committee would like to have from the minister a further statement concerning the classes of goods to which this section is proposed to be applied.
When the minister was introducing his budget he made the following statement, as reported at pages 4070 and 4071 of Hansard:
Finally, among the resolutions pertaining to tariff and customs matters, I am including a proposal which would enable the governor in council to relieve certain goods or classes of goods from special dumping duty. Under this proposal such relief could he granted in cases where the governor in council determines that the importation of the goods is necessary to meet essential requirements in Canada or could be used to advantage in Canada without causing hardship to Canadian producers. In view of continuing scarcities, it is clearly desirable that it would be possible to grant relief from dumping duty in such circumstances.
That is quite a definition the minister has given there, and before the committee approves the section, which will have the effect of giving the minister power to suspend duties with respect to undefined classes of goods, or goods the definition of which is to be made by the minister, there ought to be a clear statement from him as to the classes of goods to which it is proposed that this section shall apply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The provision to which my hon. friend is referring will in some respects give a bit more flexibility to the rigid dumping duty provisions now contained in the Customs Tariff Act. At the present time the act provides that if goods are sold in the country of origin at a price below that at which they are sold in the exporting country, then the dumping duty automatically applies to the goods imported into the other country.
There are certain cases in which the domestic price of goods may be somewhat higher than the export price, and the proposed amendment will authorize the administration, in effect, to exempt from dumping duty certain goods, under conditions that may be imposed:
The special duty imposed by the preceding subsection shall in no ease exceed 50 per cent ad valorem and the following goods shall be exempt from such duty.
The goods are:
(i)	Goods of a class subject to duty under the Excise Act;
(ii)	Goods which though of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, are not offered for sale to the ordinary agencies of wholesale or
Customs Tariff

retail distribution or are not offered to all purchasers on equal terms under like conditions, having regard to the custom and usage of trade;
(iii)	Goods or classes of goods declared exempt by any order or regulation made by the governor in council.
That is to be amended to provide that, for the purpose of this section, goods may be deemed to be of a class or kind not made or produced in Canada where similar goods of Canadian production are not offered for sale to the ordinary agencies of wholesale or retail distribution or are not offered to all purchasers on equal terms under like conditions, having regard to the custom and usage of trade.

I do not think the minister has touched the point I was raising. I appreciate the terms attaching to the power to which he has referred, but I am concerned about the type of goods to which this is to apply. Under this section the minister is to have power to select the goods; they are not enumerated in any statutory enactment. Under this section it is left to the minister to select the goods and to suspend the effect of the dumping duty as applied to such goods. We still have not had from the minister a statement as to the kind of goods to which it is proposed that this section shall apply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purpose of it is to give the governor in council power to exempt from the dumping duty in cases where the imposition of such duty would in effect impose a prohibitory tariff preventing the importation of goods which are needed in Canada and which, on their importation, will not injure any Canadian goods of a similar nature. I am told that an example of this under existing conditions might be certain types of British motorcars which are not manufactured in Canada and in respect of which the strict application of the dumping duty might require the imposition of a stiff duty on the landing of such cars in Canada, which under existing conditions are needed in the country and for which there is a ready market.
Mr. FLEMING; I take it that this section has not been introduced without there having been some demand for it in certain quarters. Surely there must be other examples than the one the minister has cited, namely British motor cars. The committee is entitled to know what classes of goods the minister has in mind when he asks us to give effect to a provision of this kind. There must be more to it than the one case of British motorcars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, while we are making every effort to increase imports of goods into Canada from what might

be generally described as soft-currency countries, the effect of our rigid anti-dumping law is to discourage some of these imports which would be brought in without injury to Canadian trade and which, as a matter of fact, would help the Canadian consumer. That is because the domestic selling price of some commodities in other countries is deliberately placed at a high figure, for taxation or other reasons, in order to discourage consumption in those countries and to encourage exports. It was felt desirable that there should be some degree of flexibility in the dumping provisions of our tariff, and that is the purpose of the proposed amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I was first going to ask if resolution 3 as amended carries.
Resolution 3 as amended agreed to.
The CHAIRMAN; Shall resolution 1 carry?
Resolution 1 agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall resolution 2 carry?
Mr. KNOWLES; I should like to ask some questions, and they are really for information, with regard to two items in the schedule to resolution 2. The items to which I direct the minister's attention are 410a and 445o. I understood from the minister's speech that any changes being proposed in the tariff were downward. I notice that in many cases there have been reductions in tariff rates, column by column. But I notice that in the case of item 410a, as it is set up in the booklet I have in front of me, the general tariff at the present time is 12] per cent and the new general tariff is to be 35 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The rates are 12] per cent, 35 per cent, 35 per cent, 30 per cent, and 37] per cent.
Mr. KNOWLES; I see. That goes down on the next page. Would the minister explain that, because it looks to me, if you have a collection of rates such as the minister has just read out-12] per cent, 35 per cent, 35 per cent, 30 per cent and 37] per cent-and you drop all those rates and put in their place an over-all rate of 35 per cent, you may in fact have provided for an increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The explanation of that is this. As of course my hon. friend knows, the general tariff is of really no consequence now. Nearly all countries are under the mostfavoured-nation tariff, and incidentally that type of material dealt with in item 410a- loading machines and so on-would come from most-favoured-nation countries. I do not think there is any general tariff country from which those articles could come. If there were,

Customs Tariff
I would think it would tend to force such countries to enter into a most-favoured-nation agreement with us. The effective tariff rates are the British preferential tariff and the most-favoured-nation tariff. There are few countries that are still under the general tariff rates. Technically it may be that the tariff rate of 35 per cent, which is one of the rates now under the general tariff, would apply; but the effective reduction is to place those things on the free list.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am glad to know that. At least it carries out the intention of the minister's tariff changes. What bothered me was, as I say, that there was at least the appearance of an increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is right there.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Here was a case where, with respect to loading machines, and so on, there was a 124 per cent rate and now there is to be a 35 per cent rate; that looked to me like a reduction in reverse.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All that stuff comes from most-favoured-nation countries or British preferential tariff countries.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I understand. The other item to which I wished to direct attention was 445o, paragraph (iii). There I noticed that all three of the rates were simply listed as "various". Now it is free, free, and 30 per cent. This is with regard to materials and parts not including motors, for use by manufacturers of apparatus using radio tubes, or parts therefor, in the manufacture, in their own factory, of the goods enumerated in tariff items 445o (i) and 445o (ii). In connection with the general tariff, previously the rate was listed as various. Now it is listed as 30 per cent. That is the only case like it in the whole schedule. Can the minister assure us that there is not an increase when it goes from "various" to 30 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I am told there is not. Here again the applicable rates are really the British preferential and the most-favourednation rates. Probably a typical case of the various rates, as I am informed by the officials in front of me, would be the ones in 445o (ii), which are 35 per cent, 30 per cent, 30 per cent, 35 per cent and 30 per cent. The 30 per cent would be the lowest of those rates. But here again in this item, the general tariff rates have really no practical application because these items are not coming to us from general tariff countries.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: So we can be assured that all the changes, where changes are made, are downward.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told by my tariff experts that that is the case.

Will the minister turn to item 410a (i), which deals with loading machines; shaker trough, belt trough, and so on. The general tariff at one time was 35 per cent. When did that general tariff cease to be effective?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When we made the first trade agreement with the United States in 1935, effective January 1, 1936.
That was in 1935. And it was reduced to what figure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At that date the United States was transferred from the general tariff to the most-favoured-nation tariff, and the rate then became 10 per cent. Before that, it had been 12| per cent.
Under the present arrangement the tariff of 10 per cent disappears?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.
Then all of the items that are listed in-what is this, the third item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Item 410a?
I was thinking of the items beginning with tariff item 15 and going on to the bottom of page 25, item 848; they have been affected by the recent change so that they all become free?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They do not all become free, no. There are varying rates which are shown on the schedule here. There are some moderate reductions in tariff in some cases. The columns in Hansard of May 18 show the proposed rates of duty and the rates in effect prior to the rates proposed by the present budget. There are varying rates there. My hon. friend can pick them out. In some cases they are free and in other cases there are reductions. Eor instance, as to item 431d, which is, engineers', surveyors', and draftsmen's precision instruments and apparatus, the previous rates were free under the British preferential tariff, 10 per cent with some at 9 per cent under the most-favoured-nation tariff and 10 per cent under the general tariff. That item is still free from British preferential countries, and 9 per cent under the most-favoured-nations tariff, and 10 per cent under the general tariff.
Yes. But in most items there has been a substantial reduction in effect where the United States is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Substantial in some cases ; in other cases, not. For instance, let us take item 410q, pumps and vacuum pumps. The
Customs Tariff

reduction in the case of the United States is from 17| per cent to 15 per cent, a reduction of 2J per cent. It varies through the schedule.
Yes; then there are other items-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are some items where there is no change. In connection with diamond drills, for instance, there is no change. It is still 10 per cent. There is a big reduction in wheel chairs.

The chairs are for the ill and the paraplegics, and everyone is grateful to the minister for having granted relief to a body of unfortunate men and women. On the whole, however, I understand that these reductions apply particularly to the United States, which has been the chief external supplier of articles appearing in the schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. Most of them are production articles-articles such as mining equipment, which enter into (the cost of production and which, by and large, are not produced in this country. I believe for many years we have been following the principle of either exempting that class of articles from duty entirely, or putting them in a reasonably low class of duty. For instance, in respect of item 410a (i), which covers loading machines, we know that kind of machinery is used in mining. It was formerly restricted for use exclusively at the face of the mine. That restriction is being deleted, because under the former item the same equipment was in many instances dutiable at a higher rate when it was used a short distance away from the actual mine face. I cite that as an example of an adjustment.

I had understood that a great deal of the plant development which has been going on in Canada since the war was to enable Canada to produce for herself many of these items, some of which appear in the schedule, and which hitherto she has been forced to import from the United States. The result of this reduction in tariff will be serious competition to Canada, and will expose to great danger our own labour market.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have been informed that in by far the greater majority of the articles in respect of which tariffs are reduced or
eliminated, those articles are of a class or kind not made in Canada.

I have one question concerning item 445o at page 22 of the resolutions. It is a complicated provision. In the first place, as I read it there would seem to be no change in sub-item (i). It is printed here only

because of the changes in sub-items (ii) and (iii). Is that not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told there is no change in wording or in rates of duty. It is a continuation of the former item 445o which provided for duty-free entry of certain named parts used in the manufacture of radio apparatus, and it is to conform to the wording incorporated in our trade agreement.
There will be no change in the tariff on radio dials?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
What is illipe butter? It is not margarine, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, it is not margarine. Illipe butter is used mainly as a substitute for cocoa butter in the manufacture of chocolates and chocolate coatings for the biscuit trade. The addition of illipe butter provides a fat that has a somewhat higher melting point than cocoa butter and which tends to prevent the bloom on, the chocolate or coating.
Imports during the next twelve months are estimated to range from 1,000 to 2,000 tons. Illipe butter is selling today at from 83 to 84 cents a pound, c.i.f. without duty, whereas the present price of cocoa butter ranges from 81.10 to $1.20 a pound.
Illipe butter is made from the illipe nut, which is found in the Netherlands East Indies, Borneo and Malaya. These nuts are processed in Holland. The illipe is a genus of a tall evergreen East-Indian tree of the family Sapotaceae.
Will the minister look at item 181b, which deals with paper in single sheets. I note the general tariff is 35 per cent. What is the reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The rate prior to the proposals in the budget under the most-favoured-nations tariff was 25 per cent, and it is reduced to 7i per cent.
Are we not very much interested in the manufacture of paper? Is this some particular type of paper?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand that this is paper which is not made in Canada. I am told the new item provides for a new type of stencil paper, now widely used in duplicating machines. The paper described in this item was provided for under order in council P.C. 6868 of September 1, 1943. The order was under the War Measures Act and lapsed on March 31, 1947. In 1946 the imports were valued at $44,950. There are no exports and no Canadian production.

Customs Tariff

With respect to item 192g, roofing felt, I note that the tariff has been changed from 224 per cent to 74 per cent, under the most-favoured-nations column. I have had representations from two mills in my county, and I have sent a letter to the minister about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have had similar representations.

Would the minister give consideration to this matter and tell my people that there is a chance that the tariff will be reconsidered. There are nine mills in Canada interested in roofing felt. There is Philip Carey Company Limited of Lennoxville, the Viceroy Manufacturing Company at London, Ontario, and the Barrett Company Limited at Jo'liette. In my county there are the Bishop Asphalt Papers Limited, and J. Ford and Company Limited.
These mills are complaining of the change in tariff and say that it will force them probably to close their doors. Since there are over 700 workers interested in those two mills, and since there is a third company, Building Products Limited, interested in this, I suggest that the minister should reconsider the matter, and not place these gentlemen in a position where they would be obliged to decrease their production. They say the market is not yet fully satisfied; but if the tariff stays in the suggested state, production from the United States will kill their market, and they will have to close their doors.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have received my hon. friend's letter and representations from the concerns to which he has referred. The information I have at the present time is that the supply situation in Canada is such that the tariff should be reduced, and that importations are required. However I am considering the matter, and if some change is desirable I shall be prepared to recommend it. I do not think at the present time, however, the mills to which my hon. friend refers will suffer any injurious consequences.
I have found that people who are affected by tariff reductions usually do fear that there may be some adverse consequences. However, the situation at the present time with respect to roofing felt is this, that I am informed that other roofing manufacturers find it difficult to obtain roofing felt from the Canadian manufacturers. That is an essential and vital building material. The information I have at the moment is that the proposed reduction in tariff is justified, but I am looking into the matter.
Has the minister any definite information that there is a shortage of this commodity?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is still tariff protection. I am advised that there is a shortage of roofing felt.

The protection is reduced
at 74 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is reduced from 224 per cent to 74 per cent; by 15 per cent. It is only the manufacturer who can import. The complaints we have received are that some independent manufacturers of roofing materials who do not manufacture their own felt are finding it difficult to get felt from Canadian roofing manufacturers. It is for that reason that the tariff is being reduced at the present time, in order to ensure supply at a reasonable cost.

The information I received from Bishop Asphalt Papers Limited is as follows:
It is quite possible that one or two of the other felt producing companies would have surplus tonnage. Toronto Asphalt Roofing Manufacturing Company is a subsidiary of U.S. Gypsum Company, one of the largest roofing and allied manufacturing organizations in the States with several felt plants and who, I believe, will shortly have in production an additional new plant of large capacity. My information is that the felt situation in the States has eased considerably in recent months so that the U.S. Gypsum might be desirous of shipping excess tonnage into Canada.
That is what they are afraid of. They are not afraid of the free entry of roofing felt from England, but they are afraid that there will be some kind of dumping from the United States. They have three grades, and the United States people can play up grade three as well as grades one or two. They can try to make people believe that grade three is as good as the other two grades. That is the way they work. These important manufacturers are afraid of that and they are asking most vehemently that the minister take this matter under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am looking into the whole question. As the committee will appreciate, roofing felt is not used by the general public; it is used only by manufacturers of roofing. The change in tariff is not on roofing but on roofing felt, the raw material which goes into the process. It is the manufacturers of roofing and also of roofing felts who are apprehensive about the reduction in duty. The other manufacturers who manufacture roofing but who have to buy their felt as a raw material are finding difficulty in getting it from the people
Customs Tariff

who manufacture both roofing and roofing felt. These representations have commended themselves to my tariff advisers. In order to enable the roofing manufacturers to get their raw materials at a somewhat lower cost, this reduction in duty is proposed. I have received representations in addition to those made by the hon. member for Portneuf; I have received representations from other manufacturers of roofing felt and roofing here in Canada which I am now studying. If I come to the conclusion that some modification is justified it will be made when the bill is brought in.

I understand that we are permitted to jump from one item to another and I should like to ask a question with reference to 445o. Back in February or March or April the radio manufacturers carried on correspondence with Mr. Callaghan who, I presume, was in Geneva at the time. One of the items under discussion at that time was that referred to in line 15 of item 445o, which reads:
High frequency iron cores with or without inserts moulded therein.
Was a satisfactory agreement made between the makers of those goods and the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that the manufacturers of these cores need the mdtal powders which come under (iii) of item 445o. These may be imported free to be used in the manufacture of these cores.
Were they not asking for a concession in connection with the metal powders to manufacture these articles?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what is being given by the proposed amendment; metal powders for the manufacture of these cores are being allowed in free.
How long will these rates of duty remain in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Until changed by parliament.
They will have to be changed by parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct, with the exception of the suspension of the textile items. Those are not under the list we are now considering.
Will any of these items be affected by the Geneva treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Some of these items are included in the trade treaty.
In the result are not these changes final; as long as we are bound by tthe treaty, we shall never be able to put the duties back where they were?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would apply only to the ones mentioned in the trade treaty. There are a few in here that are mentioned in the trade treaty.
The majority of them are mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told not.
In that regard this list is distinct from the textile list to which the minister referred earlier in the evening?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.
The minister says these can be changed at some future time by parliament, but if they are under the Geneva trade treaty they will not be changed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is nothing here
relating to the Geneva treaty. What I mean to say is that these tariff schedules are not implementing the Geneva treaty in any way.
But many of these items are in the Geneva treaty as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Only the ones which are bound, and there are only one or two here.
On those which are bound we cannot put up the duty? We cannot do that as long as we are bound by the treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would point out that any item here which is lower than the item in the trade treaty can be brought back to the trade agreement rate.
There are many items here where the margin under the British preferential is reduced. I should like to know if the British government were advised in the cases where margins are reduced?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We can bring any rate back to what it was in the trade agreements, whether it is a preferential rate or anything else.
We still have the preferential rates with Great Britain. Are_ we allowed under the existing treaties to narrow the margin between the preferential duty and the other rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have to extend the same reduction to most-favoured-nation countries in order not to widen the margin of preference, but if we wish to reverse that action and bring the rates back to what they were before this reduction, we can do so.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Customs Tariff

The rates under tariff item 410a, for instance, were British preferential, free; most-favoured-nation tariff, 10 per cent, and general tariff, 124 per cent. The new rates are British preferential, free; most-favoured-nation tariff, free, and general tariff, 35 per cent. Actually what we have done under that item is to wipe out the British preference altogether. I do not know whether we can get any of these machines from Great Britain.
Take item 410q. The old rates were British preferential tariff, 15 per cent; most-favourednation tariff, 174 per cent, and general tariff, 20 per cent. The new rates are British preferential tariff, 15 per cent; most-favoured-nation tariff, 15 per cent, and general tariff, 20 per cent. I have been wondering why the British preference has been wiped out on many of these items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have to import these goods from the United States, and it is to lower the cost to the Canadian importer. Of course it is open to us at any time to restore the duties if we want to.
The British preference has been wiped out on a good many items. Will it follow that the rates will have to remain the same when the Geneva treaties go through?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. -
We can go back under the Geneva treaties?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that is correct.
In item 192g, roofing felt, the British preference has been reduced from 15 per cent to free. Is that a bound item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it Ls not. We do not get any roofing felt from the United Kingdom.
But we have made the British preference free. It is not connected in any way with Geneva?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

I see in another item that the British preference has been dropped from 15 to 5 per cent, and that was bound. Would we not be bound for all time to come, having dropped the British preferential tariff under a bound item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that we can restore it to the rate under the Geneva treaty, whatever that may be.

You mean that if the 5 per cent was less than Geneva we could go up to
Geneva? Would the minister tell us why in 192g the British preference was dropped from 15 per cent to free?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was in order to maintain the margin of preference which existed prior to the change. We dropped the mostfavoured-nation tariff from 224 to 74 per cent, a reduction of 15 per cent, and the British preferential tariff was reduced by 15 per cent.
Why did we drop the mostfavoured-nation rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Because we wanted to import roofing felt from the United States. We are not getting it from the United Kingdom anyway. It is to reduce the cost to the Canadian consumer.

Mr. FOURNIER (Hull)1: No, but there are still three other departments. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is at hand, and I wanted to get his department in. speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I had hoped that we could have this all cleared up.
Item stands.

Special

SI. St. Mary river dam project, $2,200,000.

Will the minister outline to us how far this St. Mary river dam construction has proceeded. I notice that the estimate this year is up 8700,000 over last year. I know that last year they were putting in foundations, tunnels and things along that line. How far have they got on with the work? What is this estimate to be used for? What proportion of the construction has been completed?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There are two tunnels to be constructed in connection with the St. Mary dam to get the water around the construction. One of these tunnels has been completed, and they are about ready to start on the second.
On which side of the river?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think it is on the southeast side. I am not just sure of the direction there.
On the left bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The only one which has been started, the one which was started last year.
The left bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No, on the right bank coming down stream.
That is the left bank, as you are coming down stream on the left hand side?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes.
That would be the left bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That one is completed. There is some difficulty about the matter, which probably I should explain. It will be recalled that at the time the tenders were called for the two tunnels, there was some discussion in the house with regard to these tenders. I said at the time that we had some doubts with regard to the possibility of the bidder completing the work at the price which had been asked. That question was taken up with him by the consulting engineer, Mr. Ferguson. As a result of the discussions, he took the very strong stand that it could be completed on the basis of the tender. It has developed that it cannot be. As a matter of fact, the amount that it would have to be increased by in order to carry it out on that basis would be a price which would be higher than the second bidder put in. We have some doubts as to whether we should allow that.

Supply-Agriculture
We have had some discussion with the contractor. and this being the first contract which has been let for this kind of work, we had some hesitation in making an adjustment on the contract which would put the price up higher than the second bidder had bid. Discussions have led to the thought that probably it might be better to have the firm, which has done tile first tunnel, discontinue that work and make other arrangements for the other tunnelling. The reason is this. There is a possibility that if we permitted the adjustment to be made after the discussions which had taken place, it was thought that bidders on new contracts might have the idea that the way to get contracts was to bid them down low and get an adjustment.. It may cost us more to finish it by making some other arrangement, but we thought that in the first work we have started along this line it might be better to do that. I am not saying that it will be done in that way, but it probably will be done in that way. By making some adjustments it may cost more to get this particular job done but we think it will probably be better than to try and make adjustments now in the light of the discussions that took place.
I should like to say in regard to that, that there has been no dissatisfaction at all with the work which has been done other than that the contractor has not been able to do it as rapidly as we had hoped for. The first tunnelling is done. If any adjustment is made, it will be made with the complete understanding between ourselves and the contractor who has been on the job, and it will not put him in any bad light so far as any future contracts are concerned, if he bids on any works. I thought probably I should say that to the committee at this time in order to explain anything that might be done in connection with it in the future.
The other contract is let to a contractor named Wells, who contracted for the building of the dam. He is on the ground, and has all of his machinery there. He has been doing some work for the past summer. He is ready to go right ahead with his work as soon as we can have the tunnels completed.
Does that mean that no work will be gone ahead with excepting the tunnels until the tunnels are finished?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I doubt very much
whether any work can be done until the tunnels are through, because the water has to be taken past the dam site. At the present time, for example, if these tunnels were not in, and any construction had been done, the
amount of water that came down this stream the past spring would have taken out any work that had been there. It is almost impossible to do much work without the tunnels.
This vote is almost entirely for the other tunnel, then?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes.

Of course no work can be done on the dam until the tunnels are completed. The object of a tunnel is to provide a conveyance for the water to pass through, so that the contractor will have a dry cross-section of the river in which to start pouring his concrete or make the foundation for the dam. It is important that all the water be diverted first. St. Mary-Milk river development.
The first stage in this development has been started and a dam on the St. Mary's river is being constructed some 40 miles southwest of Lethbridge and 4 miles northwest of Spring Coulee. The dam will be half a mile long, a quarter of a mile thick at the base and 180 feet high above the river bed. The reservoir created will be 17 miles long, 6 miles wide and 176 feet deep. Its storage capacity will be some 320,090 acre feet. The dam and connecting canal should be constructed by 1949. speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The hon. member wrote me asking these questions. I am sorry that the reply has not yet reached him, although I wrote him today.
The answer to the first group of questions having to do with ithe method by which an area establishes itself to receive payment under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is, I think, as follows:
In the first place, if all other conditions are met, payments can be made on account of the flooding; and payments have been made in quite a number of townships.
On the second point, as to whether payments can be made in an area where no wheat has been harvested, and with respect to the question concerning the yardstick in such case, may I say that if grain of any kind has been seeded, there would be no question at all about the matter. If wheat is not harvested and oats and barley are harvested, or any other grain crop, then the other grain crop is substituted for wheat; and there is an established relationship so far as bushels per acre are concerned. But if there has been anything seeded and nothing at all is harvested, then it is self-evident that there has not been a four-bushel crop. Of course that would be a complete crop failure which would warrant a payment of S2.50 an acre.
The suggestion, that there may be an area where, because of flood conditions, nothing is seeded at all, leads me to say that it is difficult to conceive of there being an area of a whole township where nothing is seeded. There are probably ten acres or a thousand acres seeded somewhere. If there were no crops seeded at all, there would not be any doubt; and I do not think there would be any doubt, either, if there were not any crops, and if conditions were such that the crops could not be seeded. For example, a farmer could be paid if he did not seed any ground at all, provided that he summer-fallowed and then cultivated the land. Those provisions are all made in the regulations and in the law.
Then, in connection with river lots, it will be recalled that earlier in the session we put through legislation which made it possible for us by order in council to indicate what the units are to be. As soon as that has been established, it will apply. It applies retroactively for the present crop year; that is, the year we have just gone through.

It is the first time I have ever heard of the bonus being paid on land that was not cultivated or seeded. They have always insisted that a man should at least run a drill over the thistles or at least burn the thistles off and scratch the ground.
There is an increase of $200,000 in this item. Is that because of administration or payment of the bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We had to get a supplementary estimate last year. As my hon. friend will know, coming from almost the centre of the district, we had one of the largest drought areas there last year that we ever had, and the sum of money we had in the estimates for taking care of areas similar to those we had the year before was not sufficient, so that more money was required.	.

The minister has just said that I come from the centre of that drought district. I should like to make one more

Supply-Agriculture
appeal ito the minister to reduce the number of sections to fewer than nine, or, if possible, to pay the bonus on an individual basis. The argument used in the house before for making it nine sections was that the land was submarginal land, but, coming from that district,
I know that all ithe sub-marginal land has been eliminated in the last thirty-five years and now it is good land. A further argument was made about sandy land, but there is very little sandy land in the west. Any land thait has not had a crop did not get a crop because it did not get the rain, which will fall on some sections and miss others. This crop failure bonus takes the place of direct relief, and any time that a man needed direct relief in the township he was not barred because he lived in a section that did not get a crop. He was given relief because he needed it. This year the crop bonus came along to take care of crop failures; but just because a man is outside the township and has a row of sections in the north end, say, of another township, or on either side, he is debarred from getting the bonus. I would appeal to the minister to take into consideration that there is no possibility of these men getting any relief at all. They are denied relief by the municipality and by the provincial government, and there is no set-up to take care of them whatsoever.
Mr. GARDINER; That is the question to be discussed at ithe conference.

I hope it will be, but in the meantime these men are counting on assistance and they do not get it. The intention of the act was to take care of land which has had a crop failure. Why should we pass laws that deny them this right? They paid in the levy of one cent a bushel, and now they are out. I know the minister is a practical farmer but probably he has not seen the cases of actual hardship caused by present conditions. At the present time every section is inspected, and the inspection department is efficient. I would
again appeal to the minister to pay the bonus on an individual basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow we shall proceed with the following bills: second reading of Bill No. 228, to amend the Excise Act, 1934; second reading of Bill No. 229, to amend the Customs Act; second reading of Bill No. 327, to amend the Canada Evidence Act; second reading of Bill No. 329, to amend the Judges Act, 1946; second reading of Bill No. 326, respecting the dominion bureau of statistics. I understand that these are very small and non-contentious bills. Then we shall go into supply and consider the estimates of the Post Office Department, Trade and Commerce, and Secretary of State.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 11.30 p.m.
